name: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome
aliases: childhood epileptic encephalopathy with diffuse slow spike-wave

reference.source: ILAE classification / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Defined by a triad of multiple drug-resistant seizure types, a characteristic EEG, and intellectual impairment, usually beginning between one and eight years of age
Tonic seizures, especially in sleep, are the hallmark, alongside atonic (drop) attacks, atypical absences and frequent episodes of non-convulsive status epilepticus
The EEG shows diffuse slow spike-wave complexes when awake and paroxysmal fast activity during sleep
It is aetiologically heterogeneous, arising from structural, genetic, metabolic or perinatal causes, and may evolve from earlier encephalopathies such as West syndrome
Drop attacks cause frequent injury, so protective measures and helmets are often needed
Management usually requires broad-spectrum antiseizure medications and combination therapy, with dietary therapy, callosotomy or vagus nerve stimulation considered for refractory drop seizures
Cognitive and behavioural problems tend to worsen with ongoing seizures and are core to the encephalopathy
reference.pathophysiology: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy representing a shared final pathway of diffuse cortical network dysfunction from many underlying causes. Widespread abnormal thalamocortical synchronisation and impaired inhibition generate the characteristic generalised tonic seizures and slow spike-wave activity. Because the epileptic activity itself contributes to cognitive stagnation and regression, ongoing seizures and interictal discharges drive the intellectual and behavioural deterioration that characterises the syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: West syndrome (from which LGS may evolve)
Atypical benign focal epilepsy of childhood (pseudo-Lennox)
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep
Structural focal epilepsy with secondary generalisation
additionalInvestigations: Prolonged or video EEG demonstrating slow spike-wave and sleep-activated paroxysmal fast activity
Brain MRI to identify structural or malformative causes
Genetic and metabolic testing when no structural cause is found
Evaluation for surgical or neuromodulation options in refractory disease
redFlags: Frequent drop attacks causing recurrent head and facial injury
Prolonged non-convulsive status epilepticus with obtundation
Progressive cognitive regression accompanying uncontrolled seizures
Evolution from an earlier infantile encephalopathy signalling a severe course
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally poor, with lifelong drug-resistant seizures and significant intellectual disability in most patients. Seizure freedom is uncommon, and there is increased mortality including from injury and SUDEP, though seizure burden and quality of life can be improved with tailored therapy.
pitfalls: Labelling any child with mixed seizures and learning difficulty as LGS without the characteristic EEG features
Failing to investigate for a treatable structural or metabolic cause
Aggressive polytherapy causing sedation that worsens function without reducing seizures
Underestimating injury risk from drop attacks and omitting protective measures
management: Use broad-spectrum antiseizure medication, typically starting with sodium valproate and adding agents such as lamotrigine, rufinamide, topiramate, clobazam or cannabidiol in combination
Target drop attacks specifically with agents such as rufinamide, cannabidiol or clobazam given their high risk of injury

Consider non-pharmacological options including the ketogenic diet, vagus nerve stimulation and corpus callosotomy for drug-resistant drop seizures, and resective surgery where a focal structural lesion is identified
Provide protective measures such as helmets to prevent injury from atonic seizures
Manage episodes of non-convulsive status epilepticus and provide a rescue plan for prolonged seizures
Provide developmental, educational and behavioural support with multidisciplinary input
Investigate and address the underlying structural, genetic or metabolic cause, with genetic counselling where a heritable cause is found
